column10:
As a 4th-year student, my experience with the 2-2-1 blended learning setup so far is mixed with bad things and good things. On one hand, it’s okay because it helps me save money. I don’t have to go to campus every day, so I spend less on fare, food, and other school expenses. This is helpful for me since I also need to save for my thesis and maybe a part-time job.

But honestly, it’s also hard, especially now that I’m in my final year. We only have face-to-face classes two days a week, so our time to talk to instructors and get papers signed is very limited. I always have to plan which day my adviser or other intructors are on campus so I can submit my thesis drafts and letters. If I miss their schedule, everything gets delayed, and that’s stressful because we have many deadlines for thesis and feasibility study.

Also, sometimes our time don’t match the adviser’s consultation hours. Even if I message them, the feedback is not as good as talking in person. So even though I like that the 2-2-1 setup saves me money, I’m really struggling to manage my time and coordinate with my instructors so I can finish on time.
column15: The 2-2-1 modality has mostly affected my academic performance negatively. Because we only have face-to-face classes two days a week, my time to consult with my adviser and get papers signed is very limited, which often delays my thesis revisions and submissions.  I feel constant pressure to plan everything around those two days, and if I miss my adviser’s schedule, I lose almost a week waiting for the next consultation, so I end up rushing my work and the quality suffers.  Online messages and emails also don’t feel as effective as in-person discussions, so I sometimes misunderstand feedback or can’t explain my problems clearly, leading to more revisions and slower progress on my thesis and feasibility study.  Overall, the limited consultation time and coordination issues have increased my stress and negatively affected my pace and the quality of my outputs in my final year.
column19:
In my opinion, the 2-2-1 modality has helped a little in addressing the power and fuel crisis, but it’s not a complete or long-term solution.

On the positive side, having students go to campus only two days a week reduces the number of commuters, which means less fuel consumption and lower demand for transportation.  Fewer people on the road also means less traffic and slightly lower overall energy use related to daily travel.  For students like me, this also translates to personal savings on fare and food, which is helpful when prices are high because of the crisis. 

However, this setup doesn’t directly solve the root causes of the power and fuel crisis, such as limited energy supply, high dependence on imported fuel, or issues in the power grid.  It only reduces some demand temporarily and mainly for those who can study online.  People who still need to work onsite, run businesses, or use electricity at home continue to face high costs and possible outages, so the broader problem remains.

The biggest challenge I’ve experienced with the 2-2-1 modality is the very limited time to consult with my adviser and get important papers signed, especially now that I’m in my 4th year. Since we only have face-to-face classes two days a week, I often miss my adviser’s schedule, and then I lose almost a whole week waiting for the next consultation.  This causes delays in my thesis revisions, feasibility study outputs, and other requirements, which increases my stress and makes me rush my work, affecting its quality. 

To cope with this, I try to plan my campus days very carefully. I list all the documents I need signed and the topics I want to discuss, then I prioritize seeing my adviser first thing when I arrive on campus.  I also send my drafts and questions by email or message ahead of time, so my adviser can at least read them before we meet, even if the feedback is not as detailed as in person.  Sometimes, I coordinate with my classmates to find out which days our instructors are usually around, so I can adjust my schedule and maximize the few face-to-face days we have.  Even with these strategies, it’s still stressful, but this is how I try to stay on track despite the limitations of the 2-2-1 setup.

column10: My experience with the 2-2-1 blended learning modality has been mixed. It is a practical response to the fuel and power crisis — having fewer face-to-face days cuts down on travel costs and electricity use, which is a huge help. However, constantly switching between in-person, online, and asynchronous learning still feels tiring and confusing. It eases the burden of rising expenses, but adjusting to different formats every few days takes extra effort and focus.
column15: The 2-2-1 modality has affected my academic performance in both helpful and difficult ways. Positively, it reduces frequent travel, saving time and money amid high fuel costs that would otherwise pull my focus away from studying. Asynchronous days also let me review lessons at my own pace and manage tasks even when power is unstable. However, constantly switching between face-to-face, online, and independent learning makes it hard to keep a steady study rhythm. I sometimes miss the immediate guidance of teachers and consistent class interaction, which affects how clearly I understand some topics. Overall, it helps me stay enrolled and keep learning despite the crisis, but it also requires extra self-discipline and effort to maintain my grades.
column19: In some ways it has helped, but it is only partially effective. Reducing face-to-face days does cut school electricity use and lower commuting trips, which saves some fuel and transport costs at home. However, the savings are limited: online learning still uses electricity and internet data at home, so overall power consumption does not drop as much as expected. Also, with only two days of face-to-face classes each week, the schedule does not reduce travel enough to make a big difference in daily fuel expenses. It is a reasonable step in the right direction, but on its own, it is not enough to fully address the scale of the power and fuel crisis we face.

column21: My biggest challenges are unstable internet connection at home and the heavy travel burden on face-to-face days. At home, slow or intermittent connectivity makes it hard to attend sessions, submit work on time, and focus on lessons — compounded by household responsibilities that also demand my attention. On campus days, commuting takes long hours and costs much more amid rising fuel prices, leaving me tired before classes even start. To cope, I download all materials in advance whenever I get a stable connection and finish tasks early so poor internet won’t delay me. For travel, I plan my schedule ahead, leave very early to avoid crowds and higher fares, and rest whenever I can to keep going despite the fatigue.

column24: I recommend adjusting the balance between online and face-to-face days to better suit both students’ learning needs and real-life challenges. Right now, the schedule still leaves us burdened by heavy, costly commutes on campus days while asking us to learn from home with limited or unstable internet. I suggest reviewing the weekly arrangement — perhaps having slightly more fully remote days can cut down travel and fuel expenses, provided the school ensures learning materials are clear, accessible, and do not rely entirely on strong connectivity. Asynchronous work should be designed to be doable even with slow internet, and face-to-face sessions reserved for activities truly needing in-person interaction. This way, the modality becomes fairer, more practical, and more supportive to all students despite the ongoing crisis.
